items.title: Human-In-The-Loop en ciencia aumentada por IA: Sesgos, vulnerabilidades y evaluación. Revisión de alcance
items.abstract: La supervisión humana de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la comunicación científica se invoca con frecuencia, pero se desconoce cómo se configura y qué evidencia la respalda. Esta revisión de alcance se preguntó qué configuraciones de supervisión humana, sesgos y vulnerabilidades describe la literatura reciente sobre la coproducción entre humanos e inteligencia artificial en la comunicación científica, y qué implicaciones tienen para la evaluación de la investigación. Siguiendo PRISMA-ScR, se buscó en Scopus y Web of Science Core Collection (2020–2026; inglés y español) y se realizaron dos búsquedas dirigidas. De 385 registros de bases de datos y 18 de búsquedas dirigidas, se evaluaron 65 obras a texto completo y se cartografiaron 40 fuentes; el análisis combinó frecuencias absolutas y relativas con una síntesis narrativa por ejes, sin evaluar su calidad. El 95,0 % de las fuentes se publicó en 2025–2026 y predominaron la revisión por pares y las decisiones editoriales. Se describieron configuraciones human-in-the-loop, en las que la persona interviene en cada decisión, human-on-the-loop, en las que supervisa y puede intervenir, y sistemas sin intervención humana; human-over-the-loop solo aparece como propuesta conceptual. La evidencia aborda el anclaje, los sesgos de los modelos como evaluadores y las vulnerabilidades adversariales, con tasas muy altas de inyección indirecta de instrucciones en condiciones experimentales. La «distorsión métrica» se apoya en evidencia cualitativa. Se concluye que la presencia humana declarada no basta para acreditar una supervisión eficaz; el juicio humano previo, la separación entre instrucciones y datos y la evaluación responsable requieren validación.

items.title: Human-LLM Cognitive Extension: A Framework for Studying Coupled Cognition
items.abstract: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

items.abstract: Human–AI Charter Public Consultation: 14 Key Questions on Governability, Risk Control and Room to Develop This discussion paper invites public comment on the Human–AI Charter (Public Consultation Draft). Its central idea is to govern how AI capabilities are translated into real-world power, not intelligence itself. AI may learn, reason and research freely; but when it gains the ability to move money, operate equipment, touch infrastructure or decide on someone's behalf, that power must have a lawful source and clear limits, and stay provable, reviewable and open to remedy. The paper sets out 14 open questions in four groups: governability (G1–G4), risk control (R1–R4), room to develop (D1–D3), and legitimacy and the future (L1–L3). It also includes two candidate new clauses for consultation, not yet part of the charter text: (A) responsibility registers for high-risk AI, and (B) an independent public forum for users as a "fourth estate" of AI governance. This consultation remains open, with no closing date. Please send comments, quoting the question number (e.g. G2, R3), to humanaicharter@gmail.com. items.title: Improving AI-assisted grading reliability through explicit rubric and prompt engineering
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment and feedback in higher education has attracted growing interest, but concerns remain about the consistency and appropriateness of AI-generated grades in summative contexts. This study examined whether a combined calibration strategy involving a more explicit rubric and marking prompt could improve agreement between AI-assisted grading and educator judgement in a laboratory-based STEM assessment. We compared educator-assigned marks for 40 graduate Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems laboratory reports with marks generated by GPT-5 under pre- and post-calibration configurations, and examined agreement using complementary statistical and visual analyses. Following calibration, agreement with educator marks improved across measures of score correspondence and absolute agreement: the intraclass correlation coefficient increased from 0.818 to 0.928, the mean AI-educator difference decreased from +1.625 to +1.041 marks, and no post-calibration report differed from the educator mark by more than 10 marks. These findings suggest that the way assessment criteria, evidence requirements, and marking rules are specified can materially influence AI-human grading agreement. However, the revised rubric and prompt were introduced together, calibration drew on discrepancies observed in the same 40 reports used for post-calibration evaluation, and one educator's marks served as the reference. The results therefore support improved in-sample agreement under a human-supervised calibration strategy, rather than establishing grading validity or interchangeability for autonomous summative decisions.

items.title: Independent Research Essays on AI, Society, Power, and Structural Change: A Collection of Fifteen Analytical Works
items.abstract: DESCRIPTION This collection brings together fifteen independently authored research essays and analytical works examining artificial intelligence, social structures, political authority, economic inequality, cybersecurity, digital identity, institutional accountability, and the changing relationship between individuals and complex technological systems. Originally published as individual works through Substack, these essays approach contemporary technological and social transformations from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Some investigate technical and epistemic limitations in AI systems, cybersecurity, information infrastructure, and digital continuity. Others examine political polarization, religious authority, generational inheritance, labor-market exclusion, economic stratification, institutional recognition, and the distribution of power. Several works also explore questions concerning the reconstruction of personal identity through informational systems, the relationship between memory and continuity, and the consequences of transferring human judgment or authority into increasingly autonomous technological environments. The collection does not advance a single unified theory or claim that all included works share the same methodology. Instead, it documents an evolving independent research program organized around several recurring questions: What happens when the systems used to observe reality become incapable of representing the conditions that actually exist? How do institutions, political structures, and economic arrangements determine who receives opportunities, recognition, and the benefits of collective contribution? How are memory, identity, authority, and inherited social structures transformed when technological systems begin to mediate increasingly fundamental aspects of human life? Why do institutions repeatedly struggle to address structural vulnerabilities even when their underlying causes are already identifiable? And what forms of accountability, institutional adaptation, and technical architecture are necessary when existing systems can no longer reliably manage the complexity they have created? The works included here range from technical proposals and systems analysis to political and socioeconomic commentary, conceptual frameworks, and exploratory scenarios. Their evidentiary foundations and analytical methods therefore vary according to their respective subjects. Together, they examine a recurring structural problem: the growing distance between what complex systems represent, what institutions reward, what individuals experience, and what society is actually capable of verifying. This collection should be understood as an archival record of independent research and analysis rather than a unified theoretical framework. items.title: Industrial Internet of Agents: Conceptual Architecture, Applications, and Challenges
items.abstract: AI agents driven by foundation models have shown potential for industrial automation beyond rule-based control. However, existing studies differ in how industrial agents collaborate and how their systems are tested, making it difficult to compare networking requirements and physical execution capabilities. This paper examines the intersection of networked agents and industrial automation, where industrial signals, communication constraints, contextual information, and operational requirements must be considered jointly. It develops the Industrial Internet of Agents (IIoA) and presents a conceptual architecture for analyzing industrial deployment requirements. Building on the Internet of Agents (IoA) framework, IIoA re-specifies sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution through eleven industrial extensions. Representative studies are synthesized across shopfloor operations, autonomous plant operations and maintenance, supply chain collaboration, and digital twin systems. The analysis indicates that industrial agent networking requires the joint design of semantic coordination, operational technology (OT) interoperability, latency-aware deployment, trust governance, and verifiable physical execution. Finally, seven open challenges are identified, covering reliability, latency, protocol integrity, scalability, physical grounding, adaptability, and evaluation.

items.title: Integrating Without Conflating: A Safety-Culture-Anchored Conceptual Review of Construct Boundaries from Safety Climate to Worker Well-Being
items.abstract: Safety culture, psychosocial safety, work design and worker well-being are increasingly considered together, although they describe different organisational conditions, processes and outcomes. We conducted a safety-culture-anchored conceptual review informed by structured bibliographic searching and purposive source selection to examine these boundaries. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science on 29 June 2026 identified 3129 records. A dated duplicate audit reconciled 2500 report records; 28 verified complete texts from a 44-source conceptual set supported detailed synthesis. Recurrent organisational practices concerned management commitment, enacted priorities, resources, communication, participation, justice and feedback for improvement. Their recurrence did not establish a single higher-order construct. The synthesis compares referents, levels, mechanisms, measurement and outcomes across safety, psychosocial-health and well-being approaches. It provides explicit rules for connecting these entities without treating their measures or outcomes as interchangeable. Three conditional propositions specify future tests of construct discrimination, cross-domain pathways and diagnostic usefulness. Purposive selection, incomplete records of later selection decisions, unequal coverage of adjacent fields and the absence of documented independent duplicate screening limit coverage and reproducibility. The proposed framework is a conceptual interpretation, not a validated causal model.

items.title: Inteligência artificial e o impacto nas relações de trabalho
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y personalización del aprendizaje en la educación básica: oportunidades y desafíos. una revisión de alcance
items.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for personalized learning in basic education through tools capable of adapting content, providing feedback, and addressing diverse educational needs. The objective of this study was to analyze artificial intelligence applications in personalized learning, identifying pedagogical opportunities, implementation challenges, and research trends. Methodology. A scoping review was developed following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The bibliographic selection exercise covered publications from 2020 to 2026, considering Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and SciELO. Results. The methodological flow included 420 identified records, 90 duplicates removed, and 330 records screened. Following the screening and eligibility stages, a set of 25 studies was established for thematic synthesis. The results were organized into five categories: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence, AI literacy and teacher mediation, equity and ethics, and implementation and evaluation. The literature examined revealed opportunities related to content adaptation, individualized support, immediate feedback, and academic progress monitoring. Challenges associated with data protection, algorithmic bias, digital inequalities, and teacher preparation were also identified. Conclusions. It is concluded that artificial intelligence offers relevant possibilities for diversifying learning experiences, although its educational integration requires pedagogical supervision, ethical criteria, and contextualized evaluations to establish its actual contributions.

items.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
items.abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

items.title: Künstliche Intelligenz in der Produktionstechnik: Potenziale, Anwendungen und gesellschaftliche Perspektiven
items.abstract: This chapter conceptualizes artificial intelligence (AI) in production engineering as a sociotechnical innovation. AI not only promises efficiency gains but also fundamentally reorganizes knowledge, work, and responsibility. Three case studies from assembly planning, laser beam welding, and predictive maintenance illustrate how algorithmic systems interact with embodied experiential knowledge and which value-laden decisions are embedded in objectives, thresholds, and routines. The analysis links technical core intuitions with perspectives on tacit knowledge, rationalization, and situated practice. A synthesis reveals three key tensions: the transformation of experience into formalized model knowledge, the shift of responsibility towards system design and operation, and the change in competency profiles towards data literacy and judgment competence. Regulatory requirements and organizational governance provide the guardrails for legitimacy and safety. From this, design principles are derived for trustworthy, auditable, and empowering AI that consistently combines transparency, human oversight, qualification, and organizational embedding.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates: associations with positive acceptance and striving
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

items.title: Learning how to use a Decision Support System: a simulation of Human-AI interaction frames.
items.abstract: The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.

items.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
items.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

items.title: Lecturer Humor When AI Is at Hand: Students’ Perceptions of AI, Explanations, and Engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

items.title: Lived Experiences of Positive Solitude and AI Companion Use Among Filipino Millennials: A Phenomenological Study
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

items.title: LLM Role Configurations in Preservice Teacher Collaborative Inquiry: Differences in AI Literacy, Cognitive Load, and Discussion Dynamics
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.

items.title: Lost Between Mind, Model Collaboration, and Motion: Understanding and Measuring Cross-Model Action Misalignment in Commercial Robots
items.abstract: Embodied robots increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to interpret user intent and coordinate with robot-specific action models for physical interaction. This multi-model pipeline creates a critical semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: semantic consistency may break between what the large model understands, how the small action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what physical actions the robot ultimately performs. As a security consequence, commercial robots may execute unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands. To measure this problem, we develop TARS, a black-box framework that explores the command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors. We evaluate TARS on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, conducting 133,400 executions. TARS uncovers widespread cross-model action misalignment and achieves up to 94% verified action coverage.

items.title: Machine Governance Beyond Man vs. Machine: Toward a Theory of Situated Machine Knowing, Machine-Operational Policy, Control, and Justified Agency
items.abstract: Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.

items.title: Making learning visible in the age of generative AI: reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

items.title: Maritime Navigation Learning with Problem-Based Learning in Spherical Trigonometry
items.abstract: Background: Spherical trigonometry is essential for maritime navigation; however, conventional instruction often emphasizes procedural drills without connecting mathematical formulas to authentic bridge operations. Objective: This study examined changes in nautical cadets’ learning outcomes and perceived learning experiences following a contextualized Problem-Based Learning (PBL) intervention in spherical trigonometry. Methods: A quantitative quasi-experimental study using a One-Group Pretest–Posttest Design was conducted with 65 nautical cadets at Politeknik Pelayaran Sorong during the 2025/2026 academic year. The PBL intervention integrated authentic Great Circle navigation problems, manual calculations using the Spherical Law of Cosines, and digital cross-checking. Data were collected using pretest and posttest instruments, navigation task evaluations, and a 50-item perception questionnaire. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Modified Normalized Gain (N-Gain), and effect size (image). Results: Learning outcomes increased significantly, with the mean score rising from 59.45 (SD = 19.95) to 71.32 (SD = 22.18) (image), indicating moderate improvement (Modified N-Gain = 0.340) and a moderate-to-large effect size (image). Cadets demonstrated high computational consistency between manual and digital methods, with differences ranging from 0.000% to 0.050%. They also reported positive perceptions of conceptual understanding, motivation, self-directed learning, and collaboration, despite a slight descriptive decline in perceived problem-solving confidence. Conclusion: Contextualized PBL was associated with improved learning outcomes and high computational consistency. Given the single-group design, these findings indicate changes associated with the intervention rather than establishing definitive causality. Controlled, multi-institutional studies are recommended.

items.title: Mathematics Teacher Interaction Styles with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Personalization in Word- Problem Design
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.

items.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
items.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

items.title: Modeling the Relationship Between Psychosocial Stressor Exposure and Safety Compliance in a Developing Economy Construction Industry
items.abstract: Psychosocial hazards are established antecedents of psychological strain among construction personnel, yet whether that strain transmits exposure to safety compliance or exposure acts on compliance directly has rarely been tested with criteria sensitive to construct redundancy. This study tested these competing accounts in Pakistan, where construction carries about twice its workforce share of occupational injuries. A questionnaire survey obtained 196 responses, of which 157 were retained after screening for unengaged and duplicate cases. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was applied, with discriminant validity assessed by the heterotrait–monotrait ratio, mediation evaluated through specific indirect effects, and predictive relevance assessed out of sample. Four construct pairs exceeded the discriminant criterion before remediation, one at unity. Psychosocial stressor exposure predicted perceived strain-related safety impairment (β = 0.676) and compliance maintained under strain (β = −0.301), whereas impairment did not predict compliance and the indirect effect spanned zero under both reflective and formative specifications of exposure. Role and employment insecurity predicted compliance positively (β = 0.600), contrary to expectation. Contractors and site managers can monitor workload, scheduling, and communication conditions as early indicators of non-compliance without clinical assessment, regulators should treat work organization and employment security as safety determinants, and compliance observed under job insecurity should not be read as internalized safety commitment.

items.title: Modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa para promover el pensamiento crítico y el aprendizaje significativo en educación media colombiana
items.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.

items.title: Narrative Threat Zine-ing: Storytelling and Reproductive Privacy Communication
items.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

items.title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents
items.abstract: Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

items.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
items.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

items.title: Navigating War: Latent profiles of perceived stress and teacher emotional support in relation to agentic engagement among Kuwaiti adult university students
items.abstract: This study examined how profiles of perceived teacher emotional support, helplessness, and self-efficacy for managing personal difficulties were associated with agentic engagement among Kuwaiti adult university students during wartime. Survey responses were collected from 546 students in higher education through a cross-sectional design. The stress measure referred to the wartime period and did not directly assess war exposure or trauma. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the measurement model. Latent profile analysis identified three profiles. These were Supported-Strained, Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy, and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy. Comparisons that accounted for classification uncertainty showed significantly lower agentic engagement in the Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy profile than in both other profiles. The Supported-Strained and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy profiles did not differ significantly in the primary analysis. After adjustment for gender, however, agentic engagement was significantly higher in the Supported-Strained profile. The findings suggest that agentic engagement during wartime differs across combinations of perceived support and psychological experiences. Greater helplessness did not consistently coincide with lower engagement. These cross-sectional associations do not establish that teacher support or wartime conditions caused the differences.

items.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
items.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

items.title: Neither human nor machine alone: why the next step in AI needs an ethics core with the last word, and a receipt that proves it holds
items.abstract: Who is accountable for what an AI system does, and how can that accountability be shown rather than asserted? Human sign-off and the autonomous agent both place the last word in a single party. Following a design science approach, we built and used a third arrangement, the verification interface: human, machine and an explicit ethics core form one construct, the core has the last word over both, and every output carries a tamper-evident receipt showing what was checked. The interface has been in daily use since February 2026 and had issued 12,398 receipts by 10 October 2026. In a sealed blind test on 1798 AI answers checked against company records, its verdicts matched the answer key in 97.1% of cases; a human check of 50 answers on which two AI auditors disagreed confirmed the answer key in 44. A check took a median of 1.9 s. We derive seven design requirements, report which the interface meets, and connect the approach to EU2122, a public content profile for receipts published as an IETF Internet-Draft. The economic hypothesis, that verification per output removes the review bottleneck of AI adoption and raises speed, quality and operating margin together, is stated but not tested. The interface assumes neither that AI is conscious nor that it has moral standing. All evidence comes from one system and is reported by its developer; it shows feasibility and measured accuracy in one domain, not effectiveness across organisations.

items.title: Occupation-Specific Associations Between Psychosocial Stress and Low Back Pain Among Healthcare Workers: Evidence from Japan’s Mandatory Stress Check Program
items.abstract: Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

items.title: Occupational health and safety as a link between environmental safety and production efficiency: a moderated mediation analysis
items.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.

items.title: OpenConsult, an Open-Source Fully Local AI Scribe With Live Decision Support: Development and Formative Evaluation
items.abstract: Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

items.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Use in Secondary School Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

items.title: OPPORTUNITIES FOR USING VIRTUAL AND AUGMENTED REALITY TECHNOLOGIES IN MILITARY AVIATION
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are moving from experimental demonstrations to operational tools in military aviation. This article examines the main opportunities these technologies offer in six areas: immersive flight and mission training, cockpit and helmet-mounted displays, live-virtual-constructive training, aircraft maintenance, mission planning and debriefing, and human-performance training. Using an analytical review of academic and professional literature, the study compares the potential benefits of each application area with its principal technical and human-factors limitations. The findings show that VR offers the clearest near-term value in cost-effective procedural and tactical training, while AR offers the greatest long-term value in airborne information display and in maintenance support. Simulator sickness, latency, registration accuracy, cybersecurity and the need for validated transfer-of-training evidence remain the key barriers. The article concludes with practical recommendations for armed forces and military education institutions that wish to adopt these technologies in a phased and evidence-based way.

items.title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
items.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

items.abstract: Academic stress among university students is commonly linked to heavy assignment loads, yet the role of time management in this relationship remains contested. This study examines the effects of assignment workload and time management on academic stress and tests time management as a moderator. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among active students of Universitas Pamulang, Indonesia (n = 37, purposive sampling) using a five-point Likert questionnaire, and analysed with multiple regression and moderated regression. Assignment workload had a positive and significant effect on academic stress (β = 0.734, p < .001), whereas time management had no direct effect once workload was controlled (β = 0.081, p = .552). The model explained 62.0% of the variance in academic stress. Time management significantly weakened the workload–stress relationship (interaction b = −0.308, p = .002, ΔR² = .095). The study positions time management as a buffer rather than a direct predictor. Universities should combine coordinated scheduling of assignments with proactive time-management support.

items.abstract: Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).

items.title: Perceived Benefits and Reported Uses of Generative AI for Accessibility: An Exploratory Survey of Minnesota Educators
items.abstract: Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

items.title: Perceived impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical learning and decision-making among internal medicine residents in Ethiopia: a mixed- methods study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

items.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

items.title: Performing Trust in AI-Generated Journalism: Transparency, Authorship and Accountability in Algorithmic News Content
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

items.title: Philosophy and Education: Between Technological Convenience and Student Intellectual Autonomy in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way learners look for information, develop ideas, and complete assignments, which makes it necessary to rethink what independent thinking means. Drawing on the philosophy of education, including Islamic educational philosophy, this article addresses three questions: the nature of learners’ independent thinking, the duality of AI as either a reinforcer of reasoning or a source of intellectual dependency, and the reconfiguration of educators’ roles and learning objectives. The study is a qualitative, descriptive-critical literature review of eleven Indonesian-language journal articles published between 2023 and 2026, supported by foundational theoretical and philosophical works. It argues that AI’s effect on reasoning is not an inherent property of the technology; rather, it is likely to be shaped by the cognitive operations handed over to the machine and by the order in which AI is introduced into a learning task. Dependency is most likely when AI takes over analysis and judgment, and least likely when it is used to explain or to test the learner’s own thinking. Educators are therefore urged to design thinking processes, move assessment from products to processes, and nurture scholarly ethics such as honesty and tabayyun (careful verification). These conclusions are conceptual and call for empirical testing across educational levels.

items.title: Process Before Prompting: A Pedagogical Framework for Preserving Evaluative Responsibility When Integrating Generative AI into Creative Media Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.
