items.title: Quality Assurance Framework for AI Governance and Integration in Higher Education Accreditation: A First Operational Model for Safe AI Integration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

items.title: Relational Ecosystems in AI Workplaces: Developing a Post-Human Relations Framework
items.abstract: There is an ontological shift currently taking place in the modern workplace due to AI and collaborative technologies. The classical theories of human relations, which rely on human interaction and human co-presence, fail to explain the relational issues involved in the modern hybrid human-AI workplace environment. This paper proposes a theoretical framework known as the Post-Human Relations Theoretical Framework (PHRTF). The PHRTF is conceptualised using post-humanist organisational theory, actor-network theory, sociotechnical systems analysis, and sociology of work and technology. In light of the systematic theoretical synthesis and review of empirical papers written between 2015 and 2024, the study finds four interrelated foundations of the post-human relational ecosystem: distributed agency and relational ontology; affective infrastructure and hybrid trust; temporal-spatial dislocation and presence reconstitution; and algorithmic authority and moral accountability. The framework challenges classical human relations’ anthropocentrism, arguing that ethical, productive AI-workplace relationships require a new understanding of relational actors.

items.title: Resistance and Response as AI Literacy: What Creative-Arts Educators Can Learn from Student Resistance and Adaptation of AI
items.abstract: Today, many educational institutions are incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into their curricula, although skepticism is increasing among younger generations, particularly in Australia and the United States. Some students are organizing opposition to the use of generative AI in coursework. The creative industry continues to experiment with AI-based production methods, and art museums and film festivals are featuring AI-generated works. items.title: Revolutionizing healthcare through AI: A systematic review of applications and impacts
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology with tremendous potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to progress in medical diagnostics, clinical decision support, personalized medicine, patient monitoring, medical research, and healthcare management. This systematic review covers the current use of AI in healthcare, its clinical effects and hindrances for implementation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were followed to conduct a systematic literature search. The search query was conducted in major electronic databases using specific keywords of the studies and results, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and other sources, including studies on artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, large language models, healthcare applications, clinical decision support, medical imaging, drug discovery, digital health, and healthcare data systems. This evidence review identifies evidence of how AI is being used in a variety of healthcare areas such as medical imaging and diagnostics, virtual patient monitoring, drug design, precision medicine, rehabilitation, patient engagement, and operational health care processes. The use of AI has been shown to have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, improve clinical decision‐making, personalize care, and optimize healthcare workflows. However, there are substantial hurdles to overcome, such as data privacy and security issues, algorithmic bias, the lack of the clinical validation of AI models, regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure challenges, and the need for effective clinical validation. The key takeaways from this review are the need for a balanced approach to the integration of AI in healthcare, acknowledging both the technological innovations and the ethical, regulatory, and human factors considerations that need to be addressed. More large‐scale clinical validation studies are needed as well as the establishment of reliable AI systems and strategies to ensure responsible and fair use of AI in healthcare.

items.title: Rhythm and blues in hybrid work: Distinct working from home configurations and related HR policy demands
items.abstract: Working from home (WFH) research typically presents employees’ preferences and companies’ policies for offsite work in an aggregate manner but neglects differences between employees’ rationales in the light of how digital technology has formed their performative interaction in teams. In this paper we argue that the shortcoming results from underestimating the digital artifact as merely a passive job resource. Thus, we explore WFH preferences as contextualized construct reflecting individual, team, and technological characteristics of digital work also in their interrelatedness. Our theoretical framework adopts a sociomaterial perspective that integrates human-centric and team-centric approaches and guides the identification of distinct WFH configurations. The empirical basis consists of two cross-sectional surveys conducted in 2023 ( n = 296) and 2025 ( n = 290) among German-speaking respondents with WFH options. Using exploratory and confirmatory latent profile analyses to substantiate our configurational approach, we identify three different and robust profiles: (1) a Life Balance Profile emphasizing individual interests for offsite work while expecting HR policies supporting individual detachment, (2) a Chronos Profile emphasizing onsite synchrony with colleagues while expecting mandated same office days for all, and (3) a Kairos Profile emphasizing (hybrid) performative interaction and availability in critical moments independently from the work location. Differences between configurations can be explained by employees’ centrality of work, their digital collaboration preferences, their perceived operational team readiness, and digital competences. Notably, similar aggregate preferences for more offsite work go along with different HR policy expectations.

items.title: Safe AI Evaluation: A Systems Perspective
items.abstract: AI evaluation can involve an active, adaptive optimisation process in which AI agents re-plan, retry, use tools or delegate work to achieve a goal. Unanticipated capabilities or unsafe behaviour may emerge, and existing controls may be inadequate to prevent harm. Selected safeguards may also be deliberately relaxed to observe behaviour they would otherwise suppress, creating additional risks. This article examines the distinctive safety considerations of evaluation and their implications for control placement, observation and intervention, and presents four architectural patterns to support safe AI evaluation, including diverse supervisors, an independent verifier, silent monitoring and coordinated shutdown.

items.title: School leaders’ perspectives on teachers’ AI experiences and leadership support in South Asian schools
items.abstract: Schools across Asia are experiencing rapid educational change due to technology integration. Teachers increasingly face pressure to use Artificial Intelligence (AI), while also worrying about errors, cheating, ethical concerns, and unclear institutional policies. This study explored school leaders’ perceptions of how teachers experience AI-related anxiety and how leadership practices support teachers’ AI competence in South Asian countries. A phenomenological research design was employed. Using purposive and snowball sampling, 10 high school leaders from Pakistan, Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, and Nepal were selected. Data were collected online through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the findings. First, school leaders perceived that teachers feared accountability and public criticism when AI-generated outputs were inaccurate or inappropriate. Second, school leaders reported that teachers expressed concerns about cheating, fairness, and loss of professional identity. Third, school leaders described reducing teachers’ anxiety by creating low-risk professional learning environments and encouraging peer support. Fourth, leaders established clear guidance regarding acceptable AI use, transparency, and student data protection. Across the participating schools, leaders consistently viewed teachers’ AI-related anxiety as a major barrier to responsible AI adoption. The findings suggest that leadership practices supporting ethical AI governance, collaborative professional learning, and equitable AI implementation contribute to sustainable teacher professional development and responsible educational transformation.

items.title: SOCIAL ORDER AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: A SOCIO-ETHICAL DISCOURSE
items.abstract: People around the globe have moral values and principles. These moral values and principles govern society, since no human society practices a free-rider system. These rules and regulations form the foundation of the public good and general well-being of every society, as far as social order is concerned. Social Order, the matrix of human relationships in society, arises from the context of human nature. Human nature includes many social attributes and characteristics, such as ways of thinking and empathy. Replacing human contact with the technological term Artificial Intelligence (AI) raises serious social and ethical concerns. Ethics developed and is used because humans are corporeal, vulnerable, and empathetic. These characteristics are the basis of human social nature and, hence, societal ethics. Therefore, this paper examines the social and ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern society. The new normal, termed artificial intelligence (AI), poses significant social and ethical challenges that demand careful consideration. It can transform our society positively or negatively. To achieve this study's objective, the paper uses a phenomenological and sociological approach, theoretically framed by human nature theory. The study observes that while artificial intelligence (AI) can bring significant benefits to society, it will also affect social attributes such as thinking and empathy that human nature is endowed with. Brotherhood will be completely erased, and family ties and closeness will be destroyed. The work, however, suggests that AI must be built to align with humanity's overarching goals.

items.title: Sociotechnical Governance and Platform Exclusion: Implications for Value Creation in Urban Food Systems
items.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate urban food provisioning, but their governance architectures may create uneven conditions of participation, visibility and value creation. This study examines how Critical and Emerging Information Technologies (CEIT), digital dynamic capabilities and platform participation are associated with care-oriented value creation among neighbourhood food businesses in Medellín, Colombia. Using an exploratory-descriptive, theory-building design, the study combines a contextual documentary review with descriptive survey data from 100 businesses. The findings show partial and functionally concentrated digitalisation: transactional practices such as digital payments are relatively widespread, whereas integration with e-commerce platforms, logistics systems and advanced digital-management tools remains limited. At the same time, socially embedded value-creation practices, particularly food donations, persist but are weakly formalised and digitalised. These patterns provide evidence of limited platform participation rather than direct evidence of platform exclusion. Building on them, the study develops a relational sociotechnical model in which platform exclusion is theoretically proposed as an endogenous intervening mechanism linking CEIT configurations and digital dynamic capabilities with value-creation outcomes, while recursive mechanisms connect digital traceability, technological visibility and capability renewal. The study contributes by distinguishing digital adoption from platform inclusion, empirical participation from theoretically inferred exclusion, and socially embedded value creation from its digital visibility.

items.title: Student Learning-Support Preferences in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by students for academic support, but it remains unclear how students value AI-based support compared with other forms of teaching and peer support. This study examined learning-support preferences among 366 second-year computing students at Kaunas University of Technology who were surveyed in 2025 and 2026 using a repeated cross-sectional design. Ten learning-support preferences and GenAI use frequency were analyzed using non-parametric tests, equivalence tests, rank correlations, and ordinal logistic regression. Students rated practical examples, clearly structured information, and peer assistance highest, whereas preference for using AI tools in learning was moderate and social media was rated lowest. Between the 2025 and 2026 Software Systems cohorts, weekly or daily GenAI use increased from 58.1% to 77.1%, yet all ten preferences were statistically equivalent across cohorts and across computing programs. More frequent GenAI use was associated with stronger preference for AI-supported learning (ρ = .284; OR = 1.93, 95% CI [1.58, 2.35]), whereas its associations with peer support, group work, and most other forms of support were negligible. The findings suggest that GenAI currently functions as an additional source of learning support rather than a replacement for teaching and peer support.

Three research questions andthree null hypotheses guided the study, with the hypotheses tested at the 0.05 level of significance.The findings revealed that students’ perceptions of AI-assisted learning significantly predicted theircritical thinking skills in Chemistry (R = 0.724, R2 = 0.524; p<0.05), accounting for 52.4% of thevariance in critical thinking skills. Similarly, students’ preparedness for AI-assisted learningsignificantly predicted their critical thinking skills ((R = 0.717, R2 = 0.514; p<0.05), explaining 51.4%of the variance. Furthermore, students’ perceptions and preparedness jointly significantly predictedtheir critical thinking skills, with a multiple correlation coefficient of (R = 0.767, R2 = 0.588; p<0.05).The study concluded that students’ perceptions and preparedness for AI-assisted learning weresignificant predictors of their critical thinking skills in Chemistry. It was recommended thatuniversities promote positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning, provide adequate training to enhancestudents’ preparedness, and improve access to technological resources to support the effectiveintegration of AI into Chemistry education.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is defined in various ways. A machine that enables a more effective way to replace humans in the labor market is one way to define AI. Evaluating external inputs and using it to tackle specific tasks is another way to see AI. With the diversity of definitions, artificial intelligence is generally understood as a tool that helps solve problems, be it personal or professional. Several years ago, before the release of AI applications, people observed how AI worked via personal assistants: Cortana, Siri etc. This is how AI was used at its early stages. Companies started to adopt AI to excel manufacturing and operational tasks, minimizing expenses for labor and excluding human factor at production. Some implement AI for demand and forecast purposes. Sectors of government use AI for their own needs. Healthcare sector with the help of AI improve accuracy of determining patients' diagnoses, massive data facilitates more appropriate personal treatment. In the education sector AI is limited, because it exposes students to losing critical thinking and autonomy. However, students are being taught how to use AI, their knowledge about the technology is being greatly expanded. Focusing on fundamental principles of AI facilitates student's involvement in AI-use. In manufacturing the technology has established its efficacy, through forecast tools, machine-deviation analysis in workflow. Given its moderate cost AI became primary tool not only within big companies, but also amongst small and medium-sized manufacturers.

items.title: Technology-Mediated Language Translation for Older Adults: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Many older adults come from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities, where they frequently interact with people and services in multiple languages. Language translation technology can support their multilingual communication. This scoping review examines research on technology-mediated verbal language translation for older adults and provides recommendations for future research and practice. We identified 41 studies across six databases discussing the considerations, development, implementation, and evaluation of various technologies, including mobile apps, artificial intelligence, social robots, internet of things, and handheld translators. Research shows that current technologies offer better accessibility and availability than human interpreters and enable useful functions, including multimodal instant translation, flexible formats, and personalized features. Nevertheless, limitations remain, including mistranslations, disrupted communication, usability concerns, and technical issues. Our findings provide important evidence on the current landscape, opportunities, and considerations for future design (e.g., accuracy, usability, flexibility) and implementation (e.g., environmental control, technical appropriateness, adequate learning) of this technology.

items.title: The acmeological gamification framework for creative competence development: a testable theory for pre-service teacher education
items.abstract: Gamification in higher education has been studied mainly as a means of increasing motivation, engagement, and achievement, with far less attention to how game mechanics contribute to the creative competence of pre-service teachers. This article advances the Acmeological Gamification Framework for Creative Competence Development (AGF-CCD), a testable developmental theory of how gamified learning conditions may contribute to creative professional capability in teacher education. The framework was developed through a purposive narrative theory-building synthesis, supported by a mechanism-level evidence map in which empirical studies, syntheses, and theoretical sources are kept apart; it is neither a systematic review nor an empirical validation. It takes the well-supported link from need-supportive mechanics to autonomous motivation as a boundary premise and proposes three sequential links: autonomous motivation is channelled by interpretive feedback into reflective practice and in-task metacognitive regulation (P1); reflective practice under psychological safety and meaningful challenge activates divergent and convergent thinking (P2); and repeated, reflected creative activity in authentic professional tasks consolidates into durable creative competence, evidenced by retention and transfer (P3). Three boundary conditions concern the learner (P4a), the design, separating mechanic composition from framing (P4b), and the context, including teaching discipline (P4c). Relative to self-determination theory, the theory of gamified learning, and the interconnected model of professional growth, the framework's distinctive contribution lies in additional mechanisms (feedback architecture and consolidation), predictions that differ from those accounts (cumulative trajectory; reversal under controlling design), and explicit failure conditions. Acmeology is retained only as a falsifiable claim that development is cumulative. A validation roadmap, including a non-gamified reflective control, states how each proposition can be confirmed, qualified, or refuted.

items.title: The association between different types of anthropomorphism of artificial intelligence service agents and user trust: A three-level meta-analysis
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence service agents (AISAs) become increasingly widespread, anthropomorphism is often proposed as a way to foster user trust, yet empirical findings remain mixed. Drawing on competing trust-building and trust-undermining mechanisms, we conducted a three-level meta-analysis of 211 effect sizes from 136 independent samples ( N = 46,071) to estimate the anthropomorphism–trust association and examine its boundary conditions. The average association was positive and robust to alternative dependence models ( r = 0.462, 95% CI [0.420, 0.502]), but varied substantially across settings (95% prediction interval [−0.131, 0.811]). It was considerably weaker for objectively specified design cues ( r = 0.222) than for perception-based measures ( r = 0.543), most of which captured adjacent trait attributions such as competence and warmth. Restricting outcomes to global trust, reliance, or willingness to depend yielded a similar estimate ( r = 0.475), although construct overlap on the outcome side cannot be ruled out. Cognitive and emotional anthropomorphism were more strongly associated with trust than physical anthropomorphism in aggregate, but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for operationalization; among design cues, physical and emotional anthropomorphism did not differ significantly, and no design-based cognitive effect sizes were available. The association was stronger in Eastern than in Western samples and in survey than in experimental studies, whereas no statistically significant moderation was detected for gender composition or the prespecified service-context categories. These findings caution against reading the pooled association as a uniform effect of anthropomorphic design and suggest that anthropomorphic cues should complement, rather than substitute for, demonstrable competence and reliability in AISA design and deployment.

items.title: The Comprehension Gap in LLM-Assisted Software Development: An Experiment
items.abstract: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. items.title: The Economics of AI and Robotics: A Scenario Analysis of Automation, Employment, Poverty, Taxation and Income Distribution in a Hypothetical Three-Sector Economy
items.abstract: This study examines how the deepening of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, defined as the progressive replacement of human workers by machines, affects output, employment, poverty and income distribution. Drawing on the economics of prediction and general-purpose technologies, the task-based theory of automation, growth theory, the literature on factor shares and Keynesian demand constraints, we construct a hypothetical economy, Solvania, with 30 million inhabitants, GDP per capita of US$25,000, 6% unemployment, a 5.3% poverty rate and three sectors: agriculture (30% of output and employment), automobile manufacturing (20%) and services (50%). A macro-sectoral model linked to a 150,000-household microsimulation, implemented in Python, traces a gradual scenario, in which automation reaches 25% of jobs within five years and 50% by year 20, and a rapid scenario, in which it reaches 80% in agriculture and manufacturing and 60% in services within ten years. Both paths raise GDP strongly, to US$1.57 trillion by year 20 (gradual) and US$1.39 trillion by year 10 (rapid), but the gains are distributed very unequally. In the rapid scenario unemployment reaches 47.2%, the labour share falls from 60% to 19.9%, the Gini coefficient rises from 0.369 to 0.621 and poverty more than triples to 17.3%, while median income rises by only 8%. A policy package combining an automation levy that finances a universal dividend, universal income support, accelerated reinstatement and work sharing reduces poverty to 0.7%, lowers the Gini to 0.408 and raises GDP by a further 16%. The results are robust to alternative assumptions and support redistributive and labour market institutions established before the fastest phase of automation. items.title: The Emerging Role and Integration of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Veterinary Education: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven and algorithm-supported technological system, has rapidly expanded its role in transforming daily life and professional practice over the past decade. In this narrative review, the recent literature was examined to evaluate current and emerging applications of AI in veterinary education and practice. A previously reported PubMed-focused search and a broader literature compilation served different purposes. The historical screening counts cannot be fully reconstructed, and the synthesis was narrative rather than systematic. Veterinary schools in the United States and elsewhere have begun exploring and integrating AI into Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) curricula to support teaching, learning, and competency development. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI in veterinary education. In anatomy, AI-based visualization and interactive tools are being explored, although controlled evidence of improved learning outcomes remains limited. In digital pathology, AI-assisted image analysis can provide students with opportunities to develop skills in recognizing and interpreting pathological findings. In clinical settings, AI models have shown potential in selected imaging and clinical-classification tasks, but their educational effectiveness requires further evaluation. Despite these advances, the broader implementation of AI in veterinary education and practice faces important regulatory and ethical challenges, including concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Addressing these issues will require multidisciplinary collaboration, multicenter data integration, appropriate validation, and strong ethical governance. With these foundations in place, AI may serve as a supportive educational and clinical tool rather than a replacement for veterinary educators and professionals. In the future, appropriately validated AI tools may contribute to veterinary education and clinical training.

items.title: The Empty Chair in AI Governance: Why Human Oversight may Fail When we Need it Most
items.abstract: AI governance frameworks increasingly rely on the assurance that a “human in the loop” will provide accountability, judgment, and control when artificial intelligence systems are used in consequential decisions. This paper argues that this assurance is incomplete and potentially misleading unless organizations examine whether the human system surrounding the AI is actually capable of exercising judgment when it matters. The paper defines artificial intelligence as machine inference: computational systems that detect patterns, generate outputs, recommend actions, and simulate features of reasoning without conscience, responsibility, embodiment, or wisdom. It introduces the concept of the Empty Chair: the absence of a clearly designated owner for the formation, sustainment, and exercise of human judgment in AI-enabled decision systems. The paper proposes that meaningful oversight requires at least seven conditions: cognitive capability, behavioral authority, relational safety, decision discipline, cognitive sustainment, survivability, and relational sustainment. Drawing on applied organizational work with governance bodies, enterprise leaders, public-facing institutional systems, and cross-organizational cohorts, the paper identifies a recurring capability-authority split in which those most likely to detect certain categories of risk are not always positioned or authorized to interrupt decision momentum. The analysis further examines how automation bias and ethical fading can weaken human responsibility by making AI outputs appear more complete, objective, and procedurally sufficient than they are. The paper reframes cognitive diversity as governance infrastructure rather than a team-building concept and presents the D.E.E.P.E.R.™ practice as a structured method for recurring reflective diversification across decision cycles. It also offers practical interventions, including cognitive diversity audits, cognitive role charters, decision pause points, Empty Chair protocols, authority alignment, and recurring reflective practice. The paper concludes that AI governance cannot stop at governing machines. It must also govern the human systems responsible for supervising them. The central question is not whether a human is present in the loop, but whether that human is formed, positioned, protected, sustained, and authorized to exercise judgment under pressure.

items.title: The Future of AI & XR: How Will AI Reshape the Spatial Computing Pipeline?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how extended reality environments are created, experienced, and applied. Advances in generative AI, multimodal foundation models, spatial understanding, embodied intelligence, and wearable technologies create new opportunities across the spatial computing pipeline, but also raise questions concerning human agency, accessibility, trust, and responsible design. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from artificial intelligence, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, and extended reality to examine these developments through three complementary perspectives: AI-generated worlds for XR, human-centred interaction, and human augmentation. Invited experts will introduce these perspectives through brief position statements, followed by moderated panel discussions involving speakers and attendees. Interactive breakout sessions will enable participants to identify connections across the three perspectives, discuss open challenges, and formulate promising directions for future research. By combining expert viewpoints with active community participation, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange and initiate a broader community effort towards a shared research agenda for the future of AI and XR.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Decision Fatigue: A Study of Managerial Judgement and Workplace Efficiency
items.abstract: Managerial decision-making is central to organisational effectiveness because it influences resource allocation, employee supervision, operational planning, conflict resolution, and strategic development. In contemporary workplaces, managers are expected to make numerous decisions while handling competing priorities, digital communications, administrative responsibilities, and rapidly changing business conditions. Although decision-making is commonly regarded as a managerial competency, the cumulative demands associated with repeated decisions may receive insufficient attention. Decision fatigue is generally used to describe a perceived decline in decision-making quality, consistency, or willingness following prolonged or demanding decision activity. Its possible manifestations include postponing difficult choices, relying excessively on familiar alternatives, reducing the consideration of available options, and experiencing increased difficulty maintaining attention. However, decision fatigue is not a universally established explanation for all changes in decision performance, and its mechanisms remain subject to scientific debate. The present study examines the hidden costs of decision fatigue in managerial work, with particular attention to managerial judgement and workplace efficiency. It adopts a descriptive and analytical approach based on secondary literature relating to bounded rationality, cognitive workload, selfregulation, information overload, task switching, and organisational decision-making. The analysis explores how repeated decision demands may interact with workplace conditions such as time pressure, frequent interruptions, unclear responsibilities, excessive reporting, and poorly structured approval procedures. It also considers how decision-related difficulties may influence the consistency of managerial evaluations, the timeliness of organisational responses, employee coordination, and the use of resources. The literature-based analysis indicates that decision quality should not be understood as the product of individual mental capacity alone. It is also influenced by expertise, motivation, information quality, organisational culture, task complexity, and the design of decision processes. The study therefore recommends a balanced approach involving decision classification, appropriate delegation, structured evaluation criteria, protected concentration time, better information management, proportionate use of technology, and periodic review of organisational procedures. These measures are proposed as practical management interventions rather than as interventions whose effectiveness has been experimentally established by this paper. The study concludes that organisations should evaluate both the excellence and efficiency of managerial decisions instead of relying exclusively on decision speed or volume. It also identifies opportunities for future empirical research to establish more precisely how decision demands relate to judgement quality and workplace outcomes.

items.title: The Impact of Transformational Leadership and Organizational Culture on Employee Performance: A Study of a Selected Company in Malaysia
items.abstract: Employee performance is a central determinant of organizational productivity, service quality, and competitiveness, particularly in the fast-changing Malaysian business environment. This paper examines how transformational leadership and organizational culture are theorized and empirically associated with employee performance, and it develops a research framework and testable hypotheses for a survey-based investigation in a selected Malaysian company. Drawing on transformational leadership theory (Bass, 1985; Bass & Riggio, 2006), Schein's model of organizational culture (Schein & Schein, 2017), and social exchange theory (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005), the study positions transformational leadership and organizational culture as independent variables and employee performance as the dependent variable. A systematic review of Malaysian and international empirical studies indicates consistent positive associations between transformational leadership behaviors, particularly idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, and employee performance outcomes, as well as between supportive organizational cultures and higher performance. The paper details a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design using validated instruments (the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument, and the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire), a Krejcie and Morgan-based sample-size procedure, and a planned analytical strategy combining descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression. Four hypotheses are proposed linking transformational leadership and organizational culture, individually and jointly, to employee performance. The paper concludes with theoretical and managerial implications, arguing that Malaysian organizations seeking to improve workforce productivity should invest jointly in leadership development and culture-building initiatives rather than treating them as separate interventions. Limitations of single-organization, cross-sectional designs and directions for future longitudinal and multi-sector research are discussed.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
items.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

items.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence and digital learning platforms in enhancing ESL learners' motivation and engagement in technology-enhanced tasks. It explores how AI-powered applications, interactive learning platforms, personalized feedback, and digital educational resources contribute to students' language development, independent learning, and active participation. Particular attention is given to the influence of artificial intelligence on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The article also discusses the benefits and challenges of integrating digital technologies into English language education and emphasizes the importance of effective pedagogical guidance in creating motivating and learner-centered learning environments.
